name: Green Tourmaline
physical: Traditionally associated with a feeling of vitality
Said to bring refreshment after long, tiring days
Crystal healers link it with gentle revival of energy
summary: Green Tourmaline, or verdelite, is a vibrant forest-green gem linked in crystal lore with heart healing, renewal, steady growth and abundance.
intro: Green tourmaline, often sold under the trade name verdelite, spans every shade from pale mint to deep bottle green. Chrome-rich stones from Tanzania glow a rich emerald tone, while Brazilian crystals tend toward a cooler blue-green. Raw prisms with vertical striations are a favourite with collectors, and the polished gems are tough enough for daily wear. Good colour zoning is common, and some crystals shift from green to pink at opposite ends, creating the famous watermelon look. Gardeners and nature lovers often feel an instant kinship with this stone, because its colour recalls new leaves, moss and quiet woodland light.
history: Tourmaline's name traces back to the Sinhalese toramalli, used in Sri Lanka for coloured gem pebbles. In Europe, green tourmaline was long confused with emerald, and a few historic jewels once labelled emerald are now known to be tourmaline. The Brazilian discoveries in Minas Gerais from the sixteenth century onward produced green crystals that early Portuguese prospectors took for emeralds, a mistake that taught gemologists how to separate them. Chrome-coloured green tourmaline was found in Tanzania in the 1970s, adding an intense new green to the market. Today it is cut into jewelry worldwide and polished for crystal collectors.
meaning: Green tourmaline is regarded as a stone of renewal. Practitioners say it works on the heart in a slow, steady way, helping a person recover from disappointment and move forward with a more generous view of life. It is often used to attract money and good fortune in a patient sense: not a jackpot, but healthy habits and fruitful work. Because green is the colour of the heart chakra, healers link it with balanced giving and receiving, and with kindness toward others and oneself. Many people also place it near plants or in a garden to encourage a sense of growth. Physically it is traditionally associated with vitality and refreshment, and some folk use it as a reminder to rest, eat well and spend time outdoors.
howToUse: Keep a green tourmaline in your wallet or workspace as a reminder of long-term goals. In meditation, rest it on the centre of the chest and breathe in time with a slow count, imagining a green light spreading outward. Place a crystal beside a houseplant or in the wealth corner of a room, the far left from the door in feng shui practice. Wear it as a ring or pendant on days that need steadiness. Combined with clear quartz and citrine in a grid, it is a popular choice for projects that need patient growth.
care: Green tourmaline is hard and generally water-safe, so rinse it in lukewarm water or cleanse it with smoke, sound or moonlight. Skip ultrasonic cleaning for stones with visible fractures. Sunlight is usually fine for brief charging, though very pale stones can lighten over years of exposure, so rotate them. Wrap raw prisms in soft cloth, since the long, brittle crystals can snap, and store them away from harder gems that could scratch the polished surfaces.
identify: Genuine green tourmaline shows strong pleochroism, meaning the colour shifts between lighter and darker green as you rotate it, and raw crystals carry fine lengthwise striations. Common lookalikes include emerald, peridot, green sapphire, fluorite and green glass. Tourmaline can also be heated or irradiated to improve colour. Perfectly clean, intensely coloured cabochons at bargain prices may be glass, so ask whether treatment has been used, and compare the weight and feel of a suspected stone against a known sample.

faq.a: In crystal tradition, green tourmaline supports heart healing, patience and steady growth. People also use it to attract abundance and to feel more refreshed and energised during demanding seasons, always as a complement to practical effort.
Verdelite is the gemological trade name for green tourmaline. It covers the whole range of greens, from soft mint to deep forest, and comes mainly from Brazil, Namibia, Nigeria and Tanzania.

Green is the most common gem colour of tourmaline, so fine crystals are fairly available. The most valued are intense chrome greens and large clean stones, which command higher prices than ordinary bottle-green material.
